title: Field safety and preparation
intro: Before the first sample, make the workplace safe. Learn to notice hazards, choose protection for the actual task and explain when work must stop.

ui.practiceTitle: Inspect the site before you start
ui.practicalIntro: Perform this activity at a real site selected and checked by your trainer. The simulation does not authorize digging, handling chemicals or operating machinery.
ui.reflectionPrompt: How does planning before work protect both you and your partner? You may discuss an invented incident instead of a personal emergency.

goals: Identify hazards and justify protection for the task, using the chemical safety information when relevant.
Create a five-point checklist covering the site, tools, protection, communication and emergencies.
Demonstrate preparation, suitable protective equipment and safe tool carrying in front of a trainer.

reading.title: Safety begins before anything goes wrong
paragraphs: A sample is only useful if collecting it does not injure someone. Preventive safety means noticing and controlling hazards before work. Emergency response means acting in an organized way if something still goes wrong. This step develops prevention and preparation; the next two steps teach responses to injuries, heat illness, spills and evacuation.

Imagine that a partner becomes dizzy and confused in a remote field, or that a container of fertilizer is knocked over. Who knows where you are? How can you raise the alarm? Where can you move safely? These questions show why preparation matters. They are not an invitation to treat a casualty or clean a spill beyond your training.

Explain the purpose of today's work in your own words. If you have seen an emergency, you can reflect on what people did well or missed. You can equally use an invented example; sharing a personal experience is optional.

reading.title: 1. Look around — and consider what you cannot see
paragraphs: Before leaving the preparation area, listen to the trainer's short safety briefing. The trainer selects a safe, accessible site and confirms where sampling is permitted. Walk the route and identify uneven ground, holes, animal burrows and obstacles. Sprinkler heads at a field edge can be easy to miss and can cause a trip or damage to irrigation equipment.

Check nearby machinery, reversing alarms and overhead electrical lines. Looking down at a phone while a tractor is moving removes the attention you need to stay clear. Stay outside the working area and use the agreed safe route; do not assume that the driver has seen you.

Irrigation pipes, gas pipes and electrical cables may also be buried. An apparently clear surface does not establish that digging is safe. Do not insert a probe, auger or spade until the trainer has confirmed clearance for that location. If a marking is missing or the situation is uncertain, stop and ask. A training diagram cannot locate real utilities.

reading.title: 2. Make sure help can find you
paragraphs: Tell the supervisor where the team is going and when it expects to return. Work with a partner in remote areas and agree how to stay in contact. Carry a charged phone or the communication device specified for the site, with the relevant emergency contacts available.

A phone does not replace the buddy system. Reception can fail, a battery can run out and an injured person may be unable to make a call. Before work, agree what to do if communication fails or someone does not return. Know the access route and meeting point so you can give useful directions to help.

reading.title: 3. Know your equipment and your limits
paragraphs: Do not operate machinery just because its controls look simple. Training, permission and an appropriate supervised setting come first. Check hand tools before use: the handle must be secure, the working part sound and clean, and defects reported. Do not use a damaged tool.

Carry sharp tools so the blade or point is directed down and away from people, with enough space around you. Follow the trainer's demonstration for the particular tool; do not swing it, balance it across a shoulder near others or leave it in a walkway. Clean tools and appropriate clean gloves also help avoid contaminating the soil sample.

Before handling a fertilizer, pesticide, soil amendment or test reagent, read its label and the current Safety Data Sheet, or SDS. Older documents may say MSDS. Find its hazards, handling and storage instructions, protective measures and emergency information. Do not guess a chemical's hazards from its container colour or a test-result chart.

reading.title: 4. Plan for living things and weather
paragraphs: Watch for snakes, stinging insects and harmful plants without approaching or disturbing them. Report a hazard and use the safe route agreed with the trainer. Biological hazards are not always obvious from a distance.

Consider heat, sun and changing weather. Plan drinking water, suitable clothing, shade and rest breaks. Tell the trainer if conditions or your health change. A hat and water do not make it safe to ignore dizziness or confusion. Detailed heat-illness action is taught in the next step; here the priority is prevention and prompt reporting.

reading.title: Choose protection for the hazard — not by habit
paragraphs: Personal Protective Equipment, or PPE, is equipment worn to reduce exposure to a hazard. It supports a safe method; it does not make an unsafe site or unauthorized task acceptable. The right combination depends on the job, the material and the conditions.

Sturdy work boots provide grip and foot protection. Where impact or crushing hazards exist, the trainer specifies suitable protective toe caps, such as steel-toed boots. Long sleeves and trousers can reduce scratches, sun exposure and insect contact; a wide-brimmed hat helps against the sun. Clothing must also suit heat and the work being done.

Use eye protection selected for the hazard. Safety glasses used for particles are not automatically a substitute for chemical splash goggles. Gloves suitable for general soil work protect hands and can reduce sample contamination, but they are not necessarily suitable for a chemical.

reading.title: Chemical protection needs a compatibility check
paragraphs: For a chemical task, the glove material must be compatible with the actual chemical and exposure. Nitrile and neoprene are examples of materials, not a guarantee of protection against every product. Check the SDS and glove manufacturer's information with the trainer. Cotton or leather gloves can absorb liquid and hold it against the skin.

Compare an unused fabric gardening glove with a compatible chemical-resistant glove, using clean props only. Explain why appearance and thickness alone cannot establish chemical resistance. Check that the selected equipment is intact and suitable before putting it on.

Depending on the risk assessment, chemical-resistant coveralls or an apron may also be required. Where harmful dust, vapour or mist may be inhaled, a respirator must be selected for the contaminant and task, with the appropriate filter or cartridge and training. Tight-fitting respiratory protection requires a suitable fit test. A picture of a mask, or a dust mask used for the wrong hazard, does not prove protection.

High-visibility clothing helps other workers see you near machinery, but it does not replace separation from moving equipment. Hearing protection, such as suitable earmuffs or earplugs, may be needed near loud engines or machinery. Use the protection and working arrangements specified for the actual site.

reading.title: Bring the checks together before starting
paragraphs: Build a five-point checklist rather than a list of equipment names. First: the site and route are safe, with permission and utility clearance. Second: tools are sound, clean and carried safely. Third: protection matches the task and any chemical information. Fourth: the supervisor knows the location and return time, and the buddy and communication arrangements are clear. Fifth: emergency contacts, access, meeting point, water and weather precautions are known.

For each point, state what would make you stop. Examples include uncertain buried services, a loose tool handle, missing chemical information, a failed communication plan or a moving machine blocking the route. Report the problem and wait for a safe arrangement; ticking a box does not resolve a hazard.

Preparation, awareness and limits reduce the chance of making a bad situation worse. Completing this step does not qualify you as a first aider or certify your physical performance. Your trainer observes the practical task separately.

examples.title: A shortcut beside the tractor
examples.situation: A sampling team sees a sprinkler head and a hole on the shortest route. A tractor is reversing nearby. One partner says, “We have boots and a phone — let's go.”
reasoning: Boots reduce some injury risks, but do not remove the hole, sprinkler or moving machine.
The team stays out of the machine's operating area, reports the route hazards and waits for a safe route agreed with the trainer.
They confirm the sampling location, utility clearance, expected return and contact arrangements before carrying the tools down and away from people.
examples.takeaway: Control the route and the work first. Equipment alone is not permission to proceed.

examples.title: Two pairs of gloves on the bench
examples.situation: The task involves a liquid reagent. There are fabric gloves and nitrile gloves, but no current SDS or compatibility information has been supplied.
reasoning: Fabric can absorb a spill and hold it against the hand.
Nitrile is a possible material, but its name alone does not prove compatibility with this reagent.
Stop chemical handling and obtain the SDS, glove compatibility information and trainer's instructions. Select eye and other protection as well.
examples.takeaway: The correct action can be to stop for missing information, not choose the most convincing-looking item.

points.label: Route and ground
points.description: A sprinkler head and a burrow interrupt the route to the sampling area.
points.question: How should the team reach the area?
options: Take the shortcut; sturdy boots remove the trip risk.
Report the obstacles and use the safe route confirmed by the trainer.
Remove the sprinkler without permission to clear the path.
feedback: Boots do not remove an obstacle. Notice the burrow and irrigation fitting before moving tools.
Yes. Avoid the obstacles and protect both people and irrigation equipment.
Do not alter irrigation equipment to solve a route problem. Report it and use an agreed route.

points.label: Sampling location
points.description: The ground looks clear, but no one has confirmed whether irrigation, gas or electric services are buried here.
points.question: May you insert the soil probe?
options: Yes, because nothing is visible on the surface.
Yes, if you push it slowly.
No. Stop until the trainer confirms clearance for this location.
feedback: Buried services may be invisible. A clear surface is not clearance.
Slow movement does not establish the location of a buried cable or pipe.
Yes. Permission and location-specific clearance come before any insertion.

points.label: Machinery
points.description: A tractor is working beside the route and its reversing alarm is sounding.
points.question: What is the sound decision?
options: Keep out of its working area and follow the agreed safe route.
Walk behind it while checking your phone.
Wear a bright vest and assume the driver will stop.
feedback: Yes. Separation and attention are necessary even when you wear high-visibility clothing.
A reversing machine and distraction are a dangerous combination.
Visibility is helpful, but it is not a guarantee that the driver has seen you.

points.label: Hand tools
points.description: The spade has a loose handle. Another student suggests carrying it across a shoulder to the field.
points.question: How should you deal with the tool?
options: Use it gently; the handle will probably hold.
Report it and obtain a sound tool, then carry its sharp end down and away from people.
Carry it at shoulder height so everyone can see it.
feedback: A loose handle is a defect. Gentle use does not repair it.
Yes. Inspect first and use the carrying method demonstrated for the sound tool.
A sharp tool at shoulder height can strike someone. Visibility is not safe orientation.

points.label: Chemical information
points.description: A closed test-reagent container is on the bench. Its label is damaged and no SDS is available.
points.question: What happens before it is used?
options: Choose gloves by colour and continue.
Use the test-result colour chart to identify hazards.
Stop handling it and ask the trainer for identification, the label and current SDS.
feedback: Glove colour does not identify chemical compatibility.
A result chart is not a source of hazard or first-aid information.
Yes. Missing identification and safety information must be resolved before handling.

points.label: Protective equipment
points.description: A chemical task has been authorized, but compatibility of the displayed nitrile and fabric gloves has not been checked.
points.question: What is the best choice?
options: Check the SDS and glove maker's information with the trainer, then select the complete required protection.
Nitrile always protects against every liquid chemical.
Thick fabric is enough because it absorbs the liquid.
feedback: Yes. Match gloves and other protection to the actual chemical and exposure.
Nitrile is not universally resistant. Check the specific product and exposure.
Absorbed chemical can stay against the skin. Absorption is not chemical protection.

points.label: Contact and buddy
points.description: The team is heading to a remote corner. A phone is charged, but the supervisor does not know the route or return time.
points.question: What is still needed?
options: Nothing; a charged phone replaces a partner and check-in.
Tell the supervisor the location and return time, agree buddy and contact arrangements and plan for a lost signal.
Keep the plan private so the team can work without interruption.
feedback: Signal may fail and an injured person may be unable to call.
Yes. People must know where to look and what to do if contact fails.
Keeping the location unknown delays help. Communication is part of the task.

points.label: Weather and living hazards
points.description: The exposed field is hot, there is no agreed rest plan and stinging insects are active near the route.
points.question: What should the team arrange?
options: Continue quickly to finish before anyone feels ill.
Wear a hat and ignore the other conditions.
Report the hazards; agree water, shade, breaks and a safe route, and report symptoms promptly.
feedback: Rushing is not a control for heat or biological hazards.
A hat alone does not provide the whole plan or remove the insect hazard.
Yes. Plan for the conditions and stop to report changes rather than waiting for harm.

quiz.question: Which is a core rule before fieldwork?
options: Work as quickly as possible.
Use a phone only at breaks, regardless of the task.
Tell someone your location and expected return time.
Operate a machine if it looks simple.
quiz.feedback: Location and return information make the contact plan useful. Speed and apparent simplicity are not evidence of safety.

quiz.question: Where the task includes a risk of impact to the feet, which option is suitable when specified by the trainer?
options: Running shoes.
Sturdy work boots with suitable protective toe caps, such as steel toes.
Open sandals.
Any rubber wellingtons, regardless of their protection rating.
quiz.feedback: Footwear must match the hazard. Protective toes are needed where specified; the boot name or material alone is not enough.

quiz.question: For a liquid pesticide, how should hand protection be chosen?
options: Any leather work glove.
Any cotton glove.
Chemical-resistant gloves confirmed compatible with the product, such as suitable nitrile when specified.
No gloves if the operator is careful.
quiz.feedback: Check compatibility with the actual product. Nitrile is an example, not a universal guarantee; fabric or leather may absorb liquid.

quiz.question: For potentially contaminated soil or chemical test reagents, which item specifically protects the hands when selected for the assessed hazard?
options: Steel-toed boots.
Suitable chemical-resistant gloves.
A hard hat.
A high-visibility vest.
quiz.feedback: Gloves protect hands when suitable for the identified hazard. They do not replace the other protection or controls required for the task.

quiz.question: Where do you find detailed hazard and first-aid information for the reagents in a soil test kit?
options: On the storage shelf.
In the current SDS, also called MSDS in older documents.
Only in a general farm manual.
On the result colour chart.
quiz.feedback: Use the reagent's safety information, not a chart intended to interpret test results.

checklistModel: Confirm the route, permission and buried-service clearance; stop if any of these is uncertain.
Check clean, sound tools and safe carrying; report a loose handle or other defect.
Match PPE to the task, label and SDS; stop if compatibility or necessary protection is unknown.
Share location and return time; agree buddy, contacts and action if communication fails.
Confirm emergency access, meeting point, contacts, water, shade and breaks; report hazards or symptoms promptly.
practical: Trainer: select the accessible site, check underground services and specify permitted work, actual hazards, communication and emergency arrangements.
Student: explain the five-point checklist and identify the actual route hazards, including irrigation fittings and machinery.
Student: inspect the tools, report defects, select and put on the specified PPE, and demonstrate safe tool carrying.
Student: show how you will maintain contact and state the conditions that require you to stop and ask.
Trainer: observe the student individually, record what was demonstrated and any support needed. Stop an unsafe act; require a fresh safe demonstration before signing off the criterion.
glossary: Something with the potential to cause harm.
Personal protective equipment selected for the actual task and hazard.
Safety Data Sheet: information about a particular chemical's hazards, handling, protection and emergencies.
Working with a partner under an agreed contact and support arrangement.
Confirmation that work at a specified location can proceed safely with respect to buried services.

selfReflection.question: Can I explain workplace safety rules and choose suitable protective equipment?
selfReflection.note: This is your self-assessment, not a competence certificate.
